concepts.name: Modular arithmetic and congruences
concepts.gloss: Arithmetic on remainders modulo an integer, with a ≡ b (mod m) meaning m divides a−b.

concepts.name: Prime numbers and coprimality
concepts.gloss: Primes are integers greater than 1 with no proper divisors, and two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1.

concepts.gloss: Nonnegative integers written in base 2 as bit strings, with bitwise exclusive-or as addition of bits modulo 2.

concepts.name: Vector spaces, subspaces and dimension
concepts.gloss: Sets closed under linear combinations, described by spanning sets and bases, with dimension the size of a basis.

concepts.name: Matrices, invertibility and linear maps
concepts.gloss: Matrices represent linear maps; invertible ones can be undone, and products of matrices compose maps.

concepts.name: Permutations and bijections
concepts.gloss: A bijection of a finite set onto itself, used to rearrange the order of array entries.

concepts.name: Cartesian products and index tuples
concepts.gloss: The set of tuples with each entry from its own set, indexing multidimensional arrays.

concepts.name: Mathematical induction and recurrences
concepts.gloss: Proving statements for all sizes by a base case and a step, and solving cost recurrences of recursive algorithms.

concepts.name: Schoolbook multiplication and linear-time addition
concepts.gloss: Adding n-bit integers takes linear time, and the long-multiplication method takes quadratic time.

concepts.name: Cyclic and negacyclic indexing
concepts.gloss: Indices taken modulo N so that positions wrap around, forming the cyclic group of integers modulo N.

concepts.name: Dyadic rationals and fixed-point numbers
concepts.gloss: Numbers of the form integer over a power of two, stored as an integer with an implied binary point.

concepts.name: Sup norm and rounding error bounds
concepts.gloss: The maximum absolute value of the entries of a vector, used to bound errors so that rounding recovers an integer.

concepts.gloss: Manipulating finite sums and bounding them with standard inequalities.

background.summary: The reader has finished an undergraduate computer science degree: discrete mathematics (induction, sets, modular arithmetic, primes, permutations, binary representation), algorithm analysis with recurrences, and a first course in linear algebra (vector spaces, subspaces, dimension, invertible and triangular matrices). They know big-O, polynomials, complex numbers including roots of unity, and basic Turing machines with tapes. They have not studied the FFT-based multiplication literature, Schönhage–Strassen, Nussbaumer transforms, multitape complexity theory in depth, or numerical error analysis beyond basics.
